article.title: Winterize an Outdoor Faucet With No Shut-Off Valve
article.summary: No indoor shut-off for your outdoor faucet? Check if it's frost-free, find a hidden valve, insulate it, drain it on hard freezes, then fix it for good.
article.body:
Many older homes have outdoor faucets with no shut-off valve of their own inside, so you can't simply close it and drain the line before winter. You still have good options. This guide shows how to check what you have, protect the faucet this winter, and fix the problem for good.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: never thaw a frozen faucet or pipe with a torch or any open flame. If you use pipe heat cable, choose one that is UL- or CSA-listed for water pipes, plug it into a GFCI outlet and follow its instructions exactly.

Steps

  1. Disconnect the hose

    Unscrew the garden hose and any splitter, timer or quick-connect from the faucet. A hose left on traps water in the faucet and can split it, even on a frost-free model. Drain the hose and store it.

    Done right: nothing is attached to the faucet.

  2. Check whether it's frost-free

    Look at the pipe where it comes through the wall inside, in the basement, crawl space or garage. A frost-free faucet has a long body, usually 6 to 12 in, that reaches through the wall, so it closes in the warm part of the house and drains itself. If yours is frost-free, removing the hose is the main job: you can skip to the cover step. A standard faucet closes right at the outside wall, so the water behind it sits in the cold.

    Done right: you know whether you have a frost-free or a standard faucet.

  3. Look once more for a hidden shut-off

    Follow the faucet's pipe inward with a flashlight. In older homes the valve is often in the basement ceiling near the outside wall; in newer homes it's often next to the main shut-off. Also check behind access panels, in the crawl space and in the garage. A round handle is a gate valve; a lever is a ball valve. If you find one, close it and follow our standard winterizing steps instead.

    Done right: you have traced the pipe from the wall until it joins another line, and you're sure there's no valve on it.

  4. Fit an insulated faucet cover

    Push an insulated faucet cover over the faucet and tighten its loop or strap so the cover seals flat against the siding. A cover traps heat coming from the house and helps through short, mild freezes. On its own it won't protect a standard faucet through a long, hard freeze.

    Done right: the cover sits tight against the wall with no gap around its edge.

  5. Insulate and seal on the inside

    Where the faucet's pipe runs through a cold rim joist, crawl space or garage, wrap it with foam pipe insulation and tape the seams. Seal any gap around the pipe where it passes through the wall with exterior caulk or low-expansion spray foam, so cold air can't blow on it.

    Done right: no bare pipe is exposed in the cold space, and you feel no draft around the wall opening.

  6. Drain it from the main on hard freezes

    Before a forecast below about 20°F, or if you'll be away, turn off the main water shut-off. Open the outdoor faucet and the lowest faucet in the house to drain the line, and leave them open. With no branch valve, the line refills as soon as the main is back on, so keep the main off until the cold passes, then close the faucets and turn it on slowly.

    Done right: the outdoor faucet stops dripping, and the house water stays off until the hard freeze is over.

  7. Fix it for good before next winter

    The lasting fix is either a shut-off valve with a bleeder cap on the faucet's branch line, or replacing the faucet with a frost-free sillcock. Both mean cutting into the supply pipe with the main off. A plumber can usually do either in one visit; a confident DIYer can add a push-to-connect valve on copper or PEX by following the fitting's instructions.

    Done right: the outdoor faucet has its own shut-off, or it's frost-free.

Call a licensed plumber if: the faucet or its pipe is already frozen or leaking (turn off the main first), you see water inside the wall when the faucet runs, the main shut-off is stuck, or you want a shut-off valve or frost-free sillcock installed.

FAQ

Can I winterize an outdoor faucet without a shut-off valve?

Yes. Remove the hose, insulate the faucet and its pipe, and before hard freezes turn off the main water and drain the line. Long term, add a shut-off valve or a frost-free faucet.

Do outdoor faucet covers really work?

They help through short, mild freezes by trapping heat from the house. On a standard faucet with water in the line, a cover alone isn't enough for a long, hard freeze.

Should I leave the outdoor faucet dripping?

A slow drip can help on one very cold night, but it can freeze into ice on steps and patios. Draining the line with the main off is safer when you can do it.

How do I know if my outdoor faucet is frost-free?

Check inside where the pipe comes through the wall. A frost-free faucet has a long body, usually 6 to 12 in, that reaches into the house, and the handle often sits at a slight downward angle.

What temperature will freeze an outdoor faucet?

Water freezes at 32°F, but pipes are most at risk when it stays around 20°F or colder for several hours, especially on walls that face the wind.
